blocks.instruction: Leia o texto e escolha a alternativa correta. Algumas perguntas pedem inferência — a resposta não está escrita com todas as letras.
blocks.passage:
Executive communication in British English has a recognisable shape. It is measured. It is careful with vocabulary. It uses parallelism — three short clauses in rhythm — to carry weight without drama. It prefers concrete examples over abstract claims, and one strong anecdote over a cloud of statistics.

It also, crucially, relies on understatement. A senior British leader who is delighted with an outcome may say "I'm rather pleased with how the team handled that" — and the room understands this as high praise. Replace "rather pleased" with "thrilled" and the sentence becomes less British, not more impressive. The effect is of a voice that trusts the listener to do some of the work, respecting the audience enough to let it supply the warmth and the emotion itself.

Get this tone right and you sound as if you belong in the room. Get it wrong and you sound, however competent, as if you are still auditioning for it. The best executive voices seem effortless, yet they are deeply rehearsed: short, balanced, concrete — written the way senior British leaders actually speak.

items.q: According to the text, what does British executive communication use to "carry weight without drama"?
options: Parallelism — three short clauses in rhythm
items.why: "It uses parallelism — three short clauses in rhythm — to carry weight without drama."

items.q: Why does replacing "rather pleased" with "thrilled" weaken the effect?
options: It is too formal for a keynote
It confuses the audience about the outcome
It sounds less British and not more impressive
items.why: "the sentence becomes less British, not more impressive."

items.q: The author would most likely DISAGREE with which statement?
options: Understatement can function as strong praise.
A good executive voice trusts the listener.
Piling on superlatives makes an executive sound more authoritative.
A single anecdote can outperform a page of statistics.
items.why: Inferência: o texto argumenta o contrário — o eufemismo ("rather pleased") vale mais que os superlativos.

items.q: The contrast between "belong in the room" and "still auditioning for it" suggests that…
options: tone signals whether an executive is truly established
seniority is decided only by job title
items.why: Inferência: mesmo sendo competente, quem erra o tom parece não ter chegado lá — o tom sinaliza pertencimento.

items.q: What does "deeply rehearsed" imply about the best executive voices?
options: Their apparent ease is the product of careful preparation
They are naturally gifted and need no practice
They are read word for word from a script
They rely on improvisation in the moment
items.why: Inferência: soam "effortless", mas o esforço está escondido no ensaio — a naturalidade é construída.

blocks.instruction: Ouça Emily orientando um novo executivo antes do ensaio do keynote. Responda sem ler a transcrição — ela só aparece depois de corrigir.

audio.text:
Right, let's look at the opening again. On paper it's strong, but for this audience it's pitched a little high. You've written "We are absolutely thrilled, incredibly excited, and one hundred per cent committed." Every word is doing the same job, and the room will hear the volume, not the message.

Here's what I'd try. Keep one image, drop two adjectives, and let the rhythm carry it. Something like: "We're pleased. We're ready. And, frankly, we've done the work." Three short clauses, balanced, and the last one lands because you've earned it.

The instinct with a British board is not to reach for the biggest word. It's to reach for the truest one, and then say a little less than you feel. If you're delighted, say you're rather pleased, and trust them to read the rest. They will.

Give me two examples from the quarter — one client, one figure you're proud of — and we'll build the whole speech around those. Concrete beats grand every time in that room. And when you deliver it, don't rush the silence after your best line. That pause is the applause.
audio.label: Ouça quantas vezes precisar. A transcrição aparece depois de corrigir.

items.q: What is Emily's main criticism of the opening line?
options: Every word is doing the same job, so the room hears volume, not message
It is far too short for a keynote
It contains a factual error about the quarter
items.why: "Every word is doing the same job, and the room will hear the volume, not the message."

items.q: What concrete rewrite does Emily suggest?
options: Replace the opening with a statistic
Keep one image, drop two adjectives, and let the rhythm carry it
items.why: "Keep one image, drop two adjectives, and let the rhythm carry it."

items.q: Why does Emily ask for "one client, one figure you're proud of"?
options: To build the speech around concrete examples rather than grand claims
To compare the executive with competitors
To pad the speech to the right length
items.why: "Concrete beats grand every time in that room."

items.q: When Emily says "say a little less than you feel," she is describing…
items.why: Inferência: dizer menos do que se sente e confiar na plateia é a definição de eufemismo (understatement).

items.q: What does Emily mean by "That pause is the applause"?
options: The audience will literally clap at that point
He should end the speech there
He should wait for permission to continue
The silence after a strong line is itself the audience's response
items.why: Inferência: o silêncio bem cronometrado é o reconhecimento — não é falta de reação, é a reação.

blocks.instruction: O vocabulário da lição aparece aqui em frases novas. Escolha o sentido ou a palavra que cabe no contexto.

items.q: "Her delivery was measured throughout — never rushed, never overstated." Here measured means…
items.why: Measured (de tom) = comedido, controlado, sem pressa nem exagero.

items.q: Choose the correct word: "Instead of an abstract claim about growth, open with a ___ : the Lagos client who renewed early."
items.why: Concrete example = exemplo concreto, o oposto de uma afirmação abstrata.

items.q: "He built the whole point around a single anecdote." An anecdote is…
items.why: Anecdote = anedota: uma pequena história real usada para ilustrar um ponto.

items.q: Choose the correct word: "\"I'm rather pleased,\" she said — a piece of British ___ that the board read as high praise."
items.why: Understatement = eufemismo: dizer menos do que se sente para transmitir mais.

items.q: "The prose was clipped and precise; he trusted the reader to supply the warmth." Here warmth means…
items.why: Warmth = calor humano: a emoção que o texto deixa a plateia preencher.

blocks.instruction: Expressões e phrasal verbs que aparecem ao preparar um discurso executivo. Escolha o sentido no contexto.

items.q: "Let's tone down the opening for this audience." To tone down means to…
options: make it less extreme or more restrained
make it louder and more forceful
items.why: Tone down = suavizar, deixar menos intenso — exatamente o que Emily quer no keynote.

items.q: "The chair still has to sign off on the final draft." To sign off on means to…
items.why: Sign off on = aprovar formalmente, dar o aval final.

items.q: "A stronger anecdote would really land with this board." If a line lands, it…
options: has its intended effect on the audience
items.why: To land (de uma fala/piada) = surtir o efeito pretendido, cair bem.

items.q: "He tends to lay it on thick with superlatives." To lay it on thick means to…
items.why: Lay it on thick = carregar na tinta, exagerar no elogio — o oposto do understatement britânico.

items.q: "None of those extra adjectives will move the needle on how persuasive he sounds." This means they will…
items.why: Move the needle = mexer o ponteiro, fazer diferença perceptível.
